sections.html:
A will has to be validated by an order of informal probate or an adjudication of probate before it can prove a transfer of property or name a personal representative (SC Code 62-3-102). The main exception is the small estate affidavit, covered below. If a house sits in the decedent's name alone, the family usually needs a court-appointed personal representative before anyone can sign a deed.

There is an outer limit as well. No informal, formal testacy or appointment proceeding may start more than ten years after the death, apart from a short list of exceptions (62-3-108). After that, intestacy is treated as incontestable if nothing was filed.

sections.h2: Who can serve as personal representative
sections.html:
South Carolina ranks who gets first call on the appointment, and the person named in the will comes first. Under 62-3-203 the order runs like this:

  1. The person with priority under a probated will, including a nominee named in it
  2. A surviving spouse who is also a devisee
  3. Other devisees
  4. A surviving spouse
  5. Other heirs
  6. A creditor, starting 45 days after death, if the creditor follows 62-3-804(1)(b)
  7. The South Carolina Department of Revenue or a suitable person the court picks, starting four months after death

Anyone under eighteen is disqualified. When siblings disagree about who should serve, a house can sit unsold for months, so settle that early.

Informal probate begins with a verified application to the court. Formal testacy is a litigated proceeding started by a summons and petition. The informal application must give the applicant's interest, the decedent's name, date of death, age and domicile, and the names and addresses of the spouse, children, heirs and devisees (62-3-301). It must also state that the ten-year limit has not run.

Formal testacy decides whether a valid will was left (62-3-401). While one is pending, the court may not act on informal probate or appointment applications. A contest of an informally probated will may be brought within eight months of informal probate or one year of death, whichever is later (62-3-108(A)(2)(c)). A buyer or title company will watch that window.

Several clocks start at appointment, and a few start at death. These are the ones in the probate article.

Step (section)Deadline
Notice of appointment to heirs and devisees (62-3-705)Within 30 days of appointment
Inventory and appraisement (62-3-704(b), 62-3-706(A))Within 90 days of appointment
Creditor claims after published notice (62-3-801(a))Eight months after first publication
Outer limit for claims arising before death (62-3-803(a))One year after death
Pay allowed claims before closing (62-3-807(a))No later than 14 months after death, absent an extension

These clocks govern when a family can safely distribute proceeds. That is a separate question from when the house can be sold.

sections.h2: Can a personal representative sell the house?
sections.html:
Yes. The statute lets a personal representative acquire or dispose of an asset, land included, for cash or on credit, at public or private sale (62-3-715). The power begins on appointment (62-3-701), so a sale contract signed before the court issues letters stands on shaky ground.

At closing the title company will ask to see the letters, and a South Carolina deed from the estate is typically signed by the personal representative. If the estate distributes real property instead of selling it, the personal representative must execute a deed of distribution to evidence the distributee's title (62-3-907(A)). Heirs who inherit and then want out can sell afterward, but that adds a recording step.

Bond can matter too. It may be waived by affidavit when the estate's gross value is under twenty thousand dollars (62-3-603(B)(1)), and an interested person or creditor with a claim over five thousand dollars may demand one (62-3-605). Ask the probate court how it handles bond in your county.

A successor can collect personal property by affidavit when the whole probate estate, less liens and encumbrances, is worth no more than $45,000 (62-3-1201(a)). Real estate is the catch. The section governs collection of personal property, so a house usually needs a personal representative anyway.

  • Thirty days or more must have gone by since the death.
  • No application or petition for a personal representative may be pending or granted anywhere.
  • The probate judge of the decedent's county of domicile must approve and countersign the affidavit.
  • The affidavit is filed in that county's probate court.

A related summary route lets a personal representative close an estate not over $45,000 by sworn statement (62-3-1203, 62-3-1204), and the appointment ends one year after death if no claims or proceedings are pending.

sections.h2: How creditors are paid when the estate is short
sections.html:
When assets run short, claims are paid in a set order (62-3-805). The order matters if the house must be sold to cover debts.

  • Costs of administration, including attorney's fees and reasonable funeral expenses
  • Debts and taxes with preference under federal law
  • Reasonable medical, hospital and personal care costs of the last illness
  • Debts and taxes with preference under South Carolina law
  • All other claims

The personal representative publishes the creditor notice once a week for three successive weeks in a county newspaper (62-3-801(a)). A claim not presented in time is barred.

Inherited-house sales tend to slow down at the same few points: getting letters issued, finding the original will, agreeing among heirs, and clearing back property tax or liens. Timing and habits vary by county, so call the probate court where the decedent lived before you plan around a date.

Cash Home Buyers works with personal representatives and heirs who want to sell the house as-is. We can talk before appointment, but a closing needs someone with authority to sign. Bring the death certificate, the will if there is one, and any court paperwork you already have.

sections.h2: What a personal representative owes the heirs
sections.html:
A personal representative is a fiduciary who must settle and distribute the estate under the will and the Code, as expeditiously as is consistent with the estate's best interests (62-3-703(a)). That duty reaches a house just as it reaches bank accounts. Delay that costs the estate money, such as months of carrying costs on a vacant property, is something heirs can question.

The personal representative has the same standing to sue and be sued as the decedent had before death, except for proceedings that do not survive death (62-3-703(c)). The first person issued general letters holds exclusive authority until that appointment ends or is modified (62-3-702). Acts that benefited the estate before appointment can relate back, and the personal representative may ratify acts others did for the estate (62-3-701).

sections.h2: A faster path when one heir inherits everything
sections.html:
If the appointed personal representative is the sole devisee or sole heir, that person may distribute the estate right after publishing the creditor notice and then file a closing statement (62-3-1203(b)). The closing statement is a verified document stating the estate was fully administered and distributed, and that a copy went to distributees and known unpaid creditors (62-3-1204(a)).

Under 62-3-301(a)(7) the court may also probate a will without appointing a personal representative. Whether that helps with a house sale depends on the title company, so ask before you list or sign anything.

Most delays come from missing paperwork. Start with this list:

  • A certified death certificate
  • The original will, if one exists, since the application must say whether the original is with the court or attached (62-3-402(a))
  • Names and addresses of the spouse, children, heirs and devisees, with ages for minors (62-3-301)
  • The current deed and a recent property tax bill
  • Mortgage statements and any lien notices

If the original will is lost, the petition must state its contents and say it is lost, destroyed or otherwise unavailable (62-3-402(a)).

faqs.q: Do I need probate to sell a house in South Carolina?
faqs.a: Usually yes, if the house is titled only in the decedent's name. The will must be validated under 62-3-102, and a personal representative then has power to sell land under 62-3-715. Confirm your facts with the probate court.

faqs.q: How long does South Carolina probate take?
faqs.a: No single timeline applies. Deadlines include 30 days for notice to heirs, 90 days for the inventory, and eight months for creditor claims after publication. Allowed claims should be paid by 14 months after death unless extended.

faqs.q: Can heirs sell the house without a personal representative?
faqs.a: Generally not. A deed from the estate needs someone with authority. The small estate affidavit in 62-3-1201 collects personal property and does not by itself authorize a deed to land.

faqs.q: What is a deed of distribution?
faqs.a: It is the deed a personal representative signs to pass real property to a distributee, and it serves as evidence of that person's title (62-3-907(A)).

faqs.q: Can someone contest the will after informal probate?
faqs.a: Yes. A contest may be started within eight months of informal probate or one year of death, whichever is later (62-3-108(A)(2)(c)).
